messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Issues and pull requests
parts:
As there are more people contributing issues and patches to ggplot2, I
wanted to pass along a work around I found for (what I consider to be) a
deficiency GitHub: given an already existing Issue (say a bug report
someone has submitted) and a subsequently written patch on someone's
branch that addresses it, a pull request can not be created that is
attached to that issue. A pull request results in a new issue (though
possibly with a reference if it contains something like "fixes #xx" in
the commit message). Here is discussion of a workaround using git at
the command line:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/4528869/how-do-you-attach-a-new-pull-request-to-an-existing-issue-on-github

I suppose I should say I have not tried either the "hub" or command line
git method, but they look promising.

If this is useful to anyone, please use it; if not, ignore it.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Issues and pull requests
parts:
Thanks, this is good to know. You may want to add it to the ggplot2 wiki page about using github:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Developing-ggplot2-using-github

Also, keep in mind that sometimes you try one approach to fix something and issue a pull request, but then decide based on feedback you get that it's not the best way to go about it. For one bug, I'm currently on my third attempt (and pull request)! This may cause some problems when attaching a pull request to an existing issue. Then again, I guess it's possible in these cases to close the old issue and create a new pull request that references the old issue.

-Winston

messages.author: a79eb65f0eae8655
messages.subject: Re: Issues and pull requests
parts:
Brian and Winston,

The Github conceptual model for a Pull Request seems to be "Issue + Code": https://github.com/blog/712-pull-requests-2-0

I think the "fixes #xx" or "references #xx" is itself a suitable work-around. I guess my question is:
  1. If there's already a documented issue, and
  2. Someone else already has a pull request outstanding, then
  3. Why would a user submit a (competing?) pull request instead of commenting on the existing request?
I suppose if you really thought you could design a better patch than is in the existing pull, it's worth submitting your own pull request. But if you did submit a competing patch I'd still think a "references #xx" where xx is either an issue number or a pull request makes sense. The advantage to each request generating a new issue number is that it allows for separation of code and issues, as well as unique referencing.

Winston notes:

For one bug, I'm currently on my third attempt (and pull request)! This may cause some problems when attaching a pull request to an existing issue. Then again, I guess it's possible in these cases to close the old issue and create a new pull request that references the old issue.

I think that's exactly right: if you're revising a pull request substantially then create a new request and close the original. I've submitted a pull request, been asked to rebase, and thus closed the original and resubmitted a new request. To me, that's a totally sensible model, but I'm interested in your thoughts. 

- B
